result.question: Lesson 05 agents (ExplodeAI beginner lesson "Tool-using agent, exploded"). Primary sources only, each claim with URL, version or last-updated date, and a short excerpt (≤30 words); never fabricate; mark provider-specific facts. Questions, by stage: (1) What is an LLM agent: model in a loop calling tools; workflows vs agents (Anthropic "Building effective agents", Dec 2024); ReAct (arXiv 2210.03629, version); Toolformer (2302.04761); MRKL (2205.00445). (2) Tool definitions: name, description, JSON Schema input in Anthropic tool use docs, OpenAI function calling docs, Gemini function calling docs; why detailed tool descriptions matter. (3) The model's decision: tool_use/function-call blocks, stop_reason "tool_use", tool_choice auto/any/none/specific, parallel tool calls. (4) Argument validation: models can produce invalid arguments; strict mode/structured outputs; the application must validate. (5) Execution happens in the application (client tools) vs server tools. (6) Observations: tool_result blocks, tool_use_id, is_error, results appended to the conversation. (7) Context growth: each turn re-sends history, tool results cost tokens, context window limits. (8) Stopping: model ends turn with final answer; step limits as guards (OpenAI Agents SDK max_turns, LangGraph recursion_limit); runaway loops and cost. (9) Safety: indirect prompt injection via tool outputs (Greshake et al. 2302.12173); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications prompt injection and excessive agency; human approval for side-effecting tools; least privilege. (10) Model Context Protocol: current spec version and the tools primitive.
result.summary: The primary sources agree on a basic pattern. An LLM agent is a model running in a loop: it decides whether to call a tool, the application runs that tool, and the result goes back into the conversation as an observation until the model gives a final answer. Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (Dec 19, 2024) separates workflows, where code paths are predefined, from agents, where the LLM directs its own process. It calls both "agentic systems". The research roots are MRKL (arXiv 2205.00445v1, May 2022), ReAct (2210.03629v3, Mar 2023, ICLR 2023) and Toolformer (2302.04761v1, Feb 2023; NeurIPS 2023). Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini all define tools the same way: a name, a description and a JSON Schema for the input. All three also give a tool_choice-style control (auto/any or required/specific/none) and leave execution of user-defined tools to the application, with call IDs linking each result to its call. For stopping, the evidence is the OpenAI Agents SDK: the loop ends when the output is text with no tool calls, and max_turns guards against runaway loops. Lesson stages 7 (context growth), 9 (safety: prompt injection, OWASP, least privilege) and 10 (MCP) have no verified claims, so they need more research before they can be written.

findings.claim: Stage 1 (definition): Anthropic describes agents as systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage. It sets them against workflows, where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, and calls both 'agentic systems'. Anthropic also says agents are 'typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop'. That sentence is a description, not the formal definition. This framing is Anthropic's own.
findings.evidence: Published Dec 19, 2024. Excerpts: "Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths." / "typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop". Merges claims 0 and 1. Both votes were 3-0; one verifier rated medium only because the 'typically just' hedge was dropped.

findings.claim: Stage 1 (research roots): ReAct (Yao et al., arXiv 2210.03629v3, 10 Mar 2023, the ICLR 2023 camera-ready) has the LLM interleave reasoning traces with actions. The actions call external sources; on HotpotQA and FEVER that was a simple Wikipedia API with search/lookup/finish actions, and the results come back as Observations. Calling this 'the basic pattern behind a model-in-a-loop agent' is our interpretation, not the paper's wording.
findings.evidence: Excerpts: "generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner"; "interface with external sources, such as knowledge bases or environments"; "interacting with a simple Wikipedia API". Merges claims 2, 3, 7 and 8.

findings.claim: Stage 1 (research roots): Toolformer (Schick et al., arXiv 2302.04761v1, 9 Feb 2023; NeurIPS 2023) is a language model trained, self-supervised, to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass and how to use the results. It covers a small fixed set of tools (calculator, QA, search, translation, calendar) and inserts calls inline in its output. It is not a multi-step agent loop.
findings.evidence: Excerpt: "a model trained to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass". Merges claims 4 and 6.

findings.claim: Stage 1 (research roots): MRKL (Karpas et al., arXiv 2205.00445v1, 1 May 2022) proposes a modular neuro-symbolic architecture in which neural models are combined with discrete knowledge and reasoning modules. Calling it an early tool-augmented LLM architecture is a common reading, not the paper's wording.
findings.evidence: Excerpt: "we define a flexible architecture with multiple neural models, complemented by discrete knowledge and reasoning modules". Single source. The 'early tool use' framing is interpretive.

findings.claim: Stage 2 (tool definitions): All three providers define a tool as a name, a description and a JSON Schema for its parameters. Anthropic: name (regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$), description and input_schema, plus optional input_examples, strict and others. OpenAI: type 'function', name, description, parameters and strict; in Chat Completions these sit inside a nested function object. Gemini: a function declaration with type, name, description and parameters (type, properties, required).
findings.evidence: Anthropic: "A JSON Schema object defining the expected parameters for the tool." OpenAI: "parameters: JSON schema defining the function's input arguments". Gemini: "passed as a tool and includes: type, name, description, and parameters". None of these pages shows a last-updated date; all were accessed 2026-10-21. Merges claims 12, 15 and 20. Each field is provider-specific.

findings.claim: Stage 2 (why descriptions matter) [Anthropic-specific]: Anthropic calls detailed descriptions 'by far the most important factor in tool performance'. It recommends at least 3-4 sentences per tool, covering what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means, and caveats. OpenAI and Gemini also describe the description field as guidance on when and how to use the tool.
findings.evidence: Anthropic: "Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance." OpenAI: "Details on when and how to use the function". Gemini: "Clear explanation of the function's purpose." Claim 13. The old docs.claude.com URL now 302-redirects to define-tools.

findings.claim: Stage 3 (the model's decision) [provider-specific]: Each provider has a tool_choice control. Anthropic has auto (the default when tools are given), any, tool (one named tool) and none (the default with no tools); disable_parallel_tool_use limits the model to at most one call. OpenAI has auto (zero or more calls), required (one or more), a forced function (exactly one), allowed_tools (a subset) and none; parallel_tool_calls=false means zero or one call. Gemini has auto (the default), any, none and validated, where validated follows the schema but still lets the model reply in text. Caveat: Anthropic's page says any and tool return a 400 error on some current models, including Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, and when extended thinking is enabled.
findings.evidence: Anthropic: "With the default tool_choice of {type: auto}, Claude determines on each turn whether to call a tool or respond directly." OpenAI: "auto: Call zero, one, or multiple functions. required: Call one or more functions." Gemini: "any: Model is constrained to always predict a function call." Merges claims 11, 14, 17 and 21. Claim 11's wording 'setting tool_choice forces a call' was too broad; only any or tool forces a call.

findings.claim: Stage 3/6 (call and observation blocks) [Anthropic-specific]: When Claude calls a client tool, the response has stop_reason 'tool_use' and one or more tool_use blocks. The application appends the assistant message, then sends a user-role message holding a tool_result block whose tool_use_id matches tool_use.id. OpenAI works the same way: it returns a function_call item with a call_id, and the application sends a function_call_output that references that call_id in a second request.
findings.evidence: Anthropic: "Claude responds with stop_reason: tool_use and one or more tool_use blocks. Your code runs the operation and sends back a tool_result." OpenAI: "Make a second request to the model with the tool output". Merges claim 10 with part of claim 16. Not verified: the is_error field.

findings.claim: Stage 5 (where execution happens): The model never runs user-defined tools; the application does. Anthropic separates client tools (user-defined, plus Anthropic-schema tools such as bash and text_editor), which run in your application, from server tools (web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search), which run on Anthropic's infrastructure. OpenAI and Gemini also leave function execution to the application. OpenAI's hosted tools and Gemini's built-in tools run on the provider's side.
findings.evidence: Anthropic: "Client tools (including user-defined tools and tools with Anthropic-defined schemas, such as bash and text_editor) run in your application." OpenAI: "Execute code on the application side with input from the tool call". Gemini: "The model doesn't execute the function itself." Merges claims 9, 16 and 19.

findings.claim: Stage 4 (argument validation) [OpenAI-specific]: Without strict mode, schema adherence is best effort. With strict: true, calls reliably follow the schema, but every object must set additionalProperties: false and mark every property as required; optional fields are written as a type that allows null. If strict is omitted, the Responses API tries to normalize the schema to strict, while Chat Completions stays non-strict. Gemini's 'validated' mode is the closest equivalent. The brief also asks for the point that the application must validate arguments regardless; no verified claim covers that.
findings.evidence: OpenAI: "Setting strict to true will ensure function calls reliably adhere to the function schema, instead of being best effort." Claim 18. Rated medium because the coverage is single-provider and the 'app must validate' point is not directly sourced.

findings.claim: Stage 8 (stopping and step limits) [OpenAI Agents SDK-specific]: The runner calls the LLM. If the output has tool calls, it runs them, appends the results and loops again. It stops when the output is text of the desired type with no tool calls. If max_turns is exceeded it raises MaxTurnsExceeded; max_turns=None disables the limit, and error_handlers can return a controlled final output instead. The docs page states no default, though the SDK source reportedly uses 10.
findings.evidence: "If the LLM produces tool calls, we run those tool calls, append the results, and re-run the loop." / "it produces text output with the desired type, and there are no tool calls." / "If we exceed the max_turns passed, we raise a MaxTurnsExceeded exception." Merges claims 22, 23 and 24. Accessed 2026-10-21; the page shows no version number.

result.caveats: The lesson cannot cover these parts of the brief yet, because no claims on them survived verification: Stage 7 (context growth: re-sent history, token cost of tool results, context-window limits); Stage 9 (Greshake et al. 2302.12173 on indirect prompt injection, OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications on prompt injection and excessive agency, human approval, least privilege); Stage 10 (current MCP spec version and the tools primitive); LangGraph recursion_limit; Anthropic's is_error field; and a sourced statement that applications must validate arguments themselves. Parallel tool calls are covered only indirectly, through disable_parallel_tool_use and parallel_tool_calls. None of the vendor doc pages (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenAI Agents SDK) shows a last-updated date, so cite them with access date 2026-10-21. These pages change often: Anthropic's tool_choice restrictions on current models and Gemini's 'validated' mode are recent and may change again. The Anthropic tool-definition URL in the brief (docs.claude.com/.../implement-tool-use) now redirects; cite platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools. Wording such as 'ReAct is the basic agent pattern' and 'MRKL is early tool use' is interpretation and should be presented that way. Anthropic's workflows-vs-agents split is Anthropic's own framing.
